newsitem.title: USA: Dramatic film shows truck near Oklahoma bomb site.
newsitem.headline: Dramatic film shows truck near Oklahoma bomb site.

text.p: Prosecutors unveiled dramatic film on Wednesday showing a rental truck like the one used in the Oklahoma City bombing briefly stopping a block from the federal building and then moving off minutes before the blast.

In emotional testimony, a maintenance worker described how, minutes later on April 19, 1995, the bomb exploded and an axle flew through the air and landed on his car a block away from the Alfred P. Murrah federal building.
"I turned and saw a humongous object coming toward us, spinning like a boomerang," Richard Nichols said.

The government says the axle that crushed Nichols' car, narrowly missing his wife and nephew, was the axle from the Ryder rental truck they allege defendant Timothy McVeigh used in the bombing that killed 168 people.
Sources close to the trial said the prosecution could rest its case as early as the first part of next week, far sooner than had been expected. The defence then presents its case.
Prosecutors for the first time on Wednesday focused on the federal murder counts against McVeigh.

Elias Lopez, a Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) investigator, testified that he recovered credentials from the body of DEA Special Agent Kenneth McCullough, one of eight federal agents McVeigh is charged with murdering.
Lopez testified that McCullough was killed while performing his official duties, a requirement for being charged under the federal murder statute.
Earlier, prosecutors showed pictures taken by a video surveillance camera mounted at the Regency Towers apartment building in downtown Oklahoma City in the crucial moments before the bombing.

The grainy, black-and-white pictures clearly showed a Ryder rental truck pulled up across the street from the apartment complex and then moving off seconds later. But the truck's driver was not visible, nor was it made clear why the truck stopped.
The time, stamped on the film by the video security system, showed it leaving a few minutes before the huge bomb rocked downtown Oklahoma City.

Jurors watched the pictures with rapt attention. McVeigh had no visible reaction. McVeigh, a Gulf War veteran with strong anti-government views, pleaded not guilty to murder and conspiracy charges. He could face the death penalty if convicted.

The video sequence was narrated in court by Nichols, a maintenance worker at the Regency Towers, who was due to meet his wife and nephew outside the apartment complex at 9 a.m. the day of the bombing to go to a doctor's appointment.
Fortunately for Nichols, he was slightly late. Otherwise, he said, his voice breaking with emotion, he would probably have been driving past the Murrah building when the bomb went off.
Just as Nichols left the building, there was a "horrific explosion" and Nichols saw a huge object, an axle, flying through the air from the federal building.

Nichols, choking with emotion at times, said he pushed his wife down in the car just as the axle hit the front of the vehicle. The car was crushed but Nichols' wife and nephew, who was inside the car, survived. Only then did it dawn on Nichols that the explosion was caused by a car bomb.
Prosecutors have already introduced into evidence the mangled axle they say came from the Ryder truck.

Regina Bonny, a police narcotics agent assigned to the DEA office in the Murrah building, cried on the witness stand when prosecutors showed pictures of people she knew who died in the blast. One victim, Carrie Lenz, was pregnant and had been showing other office workers ultrasound pictures of the baby she was carrying minutes before the bomb exploded, Bonny said.
Bonny, who suffered a neck injury in the blast, wore a neck brace and said she had been operated on this week.
Jurors were then shown huge twisted metal truck parts that were found around the bomb site, but prosecutors did not immediately explain their significance.
FBI agent Patrick Daly described how teams of investigators picked up debris from a wide area around the Murrah building, collecting seven tonnes of debris that was then sifted by 80 agents.
